The prompt system was built as composable blocks: a tone block, a guideline block, and an output-format block, each versioned independently. Features assembled prompts from these blocks so about 70% of the structure was shared. We used few-shot examples for latency-sensitive features like formatting and chain-of-thought only for the higher-token-budget tasks, because CoT doubled tokens and we measured the CTR impact per feature.

The fan-out was bounded by a semaphore of three concurrent requests per user request and a per-request token budget; the vendor API had generous rate limits so the real constraint was cost. Before: p95 around 4.2 seconds for the sequential variant loop; after: p95 about 1.6 seconds, roughly the single-call latency plus scheduling overhead. Throughput on the service side dropped slightly because we were issuing three calls per request, so we capped fan-out during peak hours via a feature flag.

We measured quality with an offline set of about 1,200 labelled prompts scored on relevance and format compliance, plus a weekly human preference panel of five raters. Guardrails were regex and a small classifier for unsafe content; failures were logged to Langfuse with the prompt version so we could bisect regressions.

For the retrieval agent we chunked SOPs at 400 to 600 tokens with overlap, embedded with a Jina model, and used hybrid BM25 plus vector search with reciprocal rank fusion. The biggest win was adding document-level metadata filters so the agent only searched the relevant depot's SOPs.

The hardest tradeoff was freshness versus cost: re-embedding the whole corpus nightly was expensive, so we moved to incremental embedding keyed on document hash, which cut embedding cost by about 80% with no measurable quality change.
I would start with a thin slice: one workflow, one depot, shadow mode for two weeks, and a rubric the ops lead signs off on before anything is user facing.
